name: Chili pepper (Capsicum, red pepper) taken by mouth
short: Deaths: infant given a pepper remedy by mouth; child, 2, after biting a chilli. Oesophageal rupture, stroke, heart attack (cases). High intake linked to cancer (not proof). Trial: more adverse events.
text: This entry covers chili pepper (Capsicum, red pepper or cayenne) eaten or taken by mouth as powder or capsules, and a combination product that contains it. Capsaicin applied to the skin has its own entry. Trials: a 2023 Cochrane review found that red pepper may result in a higher risk of adverse events than placebo in functional dyspepsia (risk ratio 4.31, 95% CI 1.56 to 11.89; 1 study, 27 participants; low certainty); the abstract of a 30-person randomized trial of red pepper powder in functional dyspepsia gives no adverse-event data (the Cochrane abstract does not name its trial). In a randomized crossover study, a single dose of 2 g of chili in capsules caused more severe abdominal burning than placebo, with a trend to worse heartburn, in 15 people with non-erosive reflux disease, but not in 15 healthy volunteers. In a placebo-controlled test in outpatients with upper gut symptoms, a single capsule of 0.75 mg capsaicin (the pungent compound of chili, not chili itself) gave the 73 with functional dyspepsia a median symptom score of 10.8, against 0.5 after placebo, and 37 of them had a positive test for chemical hypersensitivity (the abstract gives this as 54% without stating the denominator). In a 12-week trial in 90 women with overactive bladder, 1 woman stopped a combination product (its form is not stated) containing chili pepper with vitamins C and D, pumpkin, Polygonum and L-glutamine because of side effects, against 8 who stopped solifenacin; the result belongs to the combination. Cancer (meta-analyses of studies of chili or capsaicin consumption; they report associations, which do not show that chili causes cancer): a meta-analysis of 13 studies (3,095 cases and 4,761 controls) found moderate-high chili consumption associated with gastric cancer (odds ratio 1.96, 95% CI 1.59 to 2.42), and its dose-response analysis found an association with high consumption (2.28, 95% CI 1.76 to 2.96) but not with moderate consumption (0.72, 95% CI 0.36 to 1.41); a meta-analysis of 16 studies (8,337 cases) found an odds ratio for gastric cancer of 1.51 (95% CI 1.02 to 2.00) for the highest against the lowest consumption in all countries, 2.05 (95% CI 1.15 to 2.95) for Mexico, 2.03 (95% CI 0.71 to 3.34) for Colombia and 1.92 (95% CI 1.21 to 2.64) for Asian countries, but 0.48 (95% CI 0.24 to 0.72) for other countries, and its dose-response analysis found a positive linear correlation between gastric cancer risk and the daily frequency of chili consumption; a meta-analysis of 14 case-control studies (5,009 gastrointestinal cancers among 11,310 participants) found high consumption associated with gastrointestinal cancers overall (1.64, 95% CI 1.00 to 2.70) and chili consumption associated with oesophageal cancer (2.71, 95% CI 1.54 to 4.75), but no statistically significant association with gastric or colorectal cancer; for gastrointestinal cancers overall, its associations were positive in Asian, African and North American studies and inverse in South American and European studies; and a meta-analysis of 10 case-control studies (2,452 cases and 3,996 controls) of capsaicin intake found lower odds of gastric cancer with low intake (odds ratio 0.55) and higher odds with medium-high intake (1.94). None of these abstracts describes chili powder or capsules taken as a remedy. Case reports: a healthy 2-year-old girl accidentally bit a green chilli, vomited repeatedly, became unconscious and died the next day; autopsy showed respiratory failure from acute respiratory distress syndrome after she inhaled stomach contents. A healthy 15-year-old boy ate one of the spiciest peppers on a dare and 2 days later had an acute cerebellar infarct (stroke) with reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (temporary narrowing of brain arteries). A 47-year-old man who ate ghost peppers in a contest had violent retching and vomiting and a 2.5-cm tear of the lower oesophagus, needing surgery, with discharge on day 23. A previously healthy 25-year-old man who had recently started cayenne pepper pills for slimming had an extensive heart attack with open (unblocked) coronary arteries, which the authors attribute to coronary artery spasm. Case reports also describe a hypertensive crisis in a 19-year-old man, and a hypertensive crisis with a heart attack in a 59-year-old man with a raised thyroid-stimulating hormone level, each the day after eating large amounts of peppers and chili peppers; and severe abdominal pain needing hospital admission, resolving within 30 hours, in a 27-year-old man who swallowed an estimated 600 mg or more of capsaicin in a spicy-food contest. An undigested green chilli caused small-bowel obstruction with a localised perforation of the ileum in a 43-year-old man (a case report). A record with no abstract is titled 'Anaphylaxis to pickled chili pepper (Capsicum frutescens)'; the patient and the outcome cannot be reported. A review's title reports a case of hot peppers used in child abuse; its abstract gives no details of the case. Infants and children: an 8-month-old infant died after being given a traditional remedy by mouth as an infusion of a red powder, in which laboratory analysis confirmed capsaicin; the infant had coughing with diarrhoea and vomiting on admission, and the authors say pepper preparations used as traditional medicines are highly toxic and their use in infants should be discouraged (a case report). Besides this and the fatal chilli bite above, a record with no abstract is titled 'Air leak syndrome and respiratory distress after green chilli aspiration in a child' (title only); a case report describes a short-lived red rash in 2 breast-fed infants after their mothers ate food flavoured with red pepper, and a 17-month-old boy had hives, conjunctivitis, facial swelling and severe cough immediately after food in a spiced marinade containing black and cayenne pepper, with positive skin tests to cayenne and black pepper. Interactions and bleeding: in a prospective 16-week diary study of 171 adults taking the blood thinner warfarin, cayenne was among the complementary products associated with an increased risk of self-reported bleeding, but only two products, coenzyme Q10 and ginger, were independently associated with it; these are associations, not proof of cause. A 2026 case report describes a 50-year-old man taking aspirin, fish oil and high-dose cayenne pepper supplements who, after starting anticoagulant treatment for a deep vein clot, developed a rapidly expanding bleed within a muscle with compartment syndrome needing emergency surgery and a further operation; the authors list at least six risk factors, including platelet-modifying supplements, and say the same outcome could plausibly have resulted from the anticoagulant alone.
